title: UX and Growth shouldn't work apart
description: UX and Growth try to answer the same question from different angles. Where the two meet and why working together drives better results.

related.title: Clint Acquire
related.body: In practice: a landing page and a conversational flow that captured 79% of sales demand.

data.intro: For a long time, UX and Growth were treated as separate areas inside a product.
data.ux: On one side, UX thinking about research, usability, journey and experience.
data.growth: On the other, Growth looking at acquisition, conversion, activation and retention.
data.bridge: But in the end, both are trying to answer very similar questions:
data.question: What makes a person use a product, keep using it and see value in it?
data.view: The difference is often just the point of view.
data.growthSees: Growth looks at the numbers and spots where there's an opportunity.
data.uxSees: UX tries to understand the behavior and the reasons behind those numbers.
data.close: And it's exactly in that combination that I believe product teams have a huge opportunity.

blocks.text: UX doesn't end at the experience
When we talk about UX, people usually think about usability, information architecture, interface and journey.
All of that still matters.
But the experience also directly shapes the product's results.
Picture a sign-up flow where lots of people start, but few finish.
The Growth team can spot a drop in conversion.
But the number alone doesn't explain the problem.
That's when UX can help investigate:
Is the form too long?
Do people not understand why they need to share that information?
Is there a step that makes people feel unsure?
Does the user not see the benefit of moving forward?
Is there an accessibility issue?
Maybe the fix isn't just changing a button color or adding a new CTA.
Before thinking about the solution, we need to understand the behavior.
Growth shouldn't look only at conversion either
By the same token, Growth shouldn't be seen as just the team in charge of making numbers go up.
Conversion matters.
But a conversion on its own doesn't tell the whole story.
We can raise a conversion rate and, at the same time, create a bad experience.
We can get more sign-ups but have fewer people reaching the first moment of value.
We can increase sales, but also increase churn.
That's why looking at a single metric can push the team toward a decision that looks good on the dashboard but isn't necessarily good for the product.

data.lead: This is where a fuller view of the journey comes in.
data.after: Every stage is tied to the user experience.

blocks.text: Where UX meets Growth
Think of a digital product getting plenty of traffic, but few people signing up.

blocks.caption: Growth shows where to look; UX explains why.

blocks.text: Growth can look at the page's conversion rate.
UX can analyze the value proposition, the content, the visual hierarchy, how clear the information is, and even talk to users to understand what's blocking the decision.
Now imagine lots of people sign up, but few actually use the product.
The problem changed.
Maybe it's no longer acquisition or conversion.
It might be in the onboarding.
Maybe the user doesn't know what to do after signing up.
Maybe the product is showing too much information at once.
Maybe the user just didn't see the value.
In this scenario, UX and Growth can work together to find the cause and test different solutions.

data.after: That second question can lead to much better decisions.

blocks.text: Data shows what's happening. UX helps you understand why.
This is one of the points I find most important.
Quantitative data is essential for understanding behavior at scale.
We might find out that:

items: 40% of people drop off at a certain step;
the onboarding has a big drop at the second step;
a certain page has a lower CTR;
users with a certain profile retain better;

blocks.text: But there's a difference between knowing what's happening and understanding why it's happening.
That's where research, interviews, usability tests, behavior analysis and other qualitative methods come in.
The two sides complement each other.
Data can show where to dig.
Research can help you understand the problem.
And tests can help you find out whether the solution actually works.

blocks.caption: Data shows where to dig, research explains why, and testing shows whether the solution works.

blocks.text: Designers need to understand the business too
I believe this is one of the biggest moves a Product Designer can make in their career.
We don't need to turn designers into Growth specialists.
But we do need to understand how our decisions impact the product.
When we understand metrics like:
CTR, conversion, activation, retention, churn, LTV and CAC, we can take part in conversations that go beyond the interface.
It also changes how we present our work.
Instead of saying:
“I redesigned this screen to improve the experience.”
We can explain:
“We found friction at this stage of the journey, looked into user behavior and built a solution to reduce that friction and improve activation.”
The second conversation is much closer to product.
Not every improvement has to be visual
This is another point I find important.
When a metric looks bad, the first reaction is often to tweak the interface.
But maybe the problem isn't in the interface.

items: It could be the value proposition
The moment the information shows up
A process that's way too complicated

blocks.text: Or simply the fact that the product doesn't solve a need that matters enough.
That's why UX and Growth need to work on the problem before working on the solution.
Experimenting is part of UX work too
Getting closer to Growth can also change the way we think about design.

blocks.caption: Experimenting is part of UX work, not just Growth's.

blocks.text: Instead of spending weeks trying to find the perfect solution, we can form hypotheses, prototype, test and learn.
For example:
Hypothesis: users drop the sign-up because they don't understand why a certain piece of information is needed.
Solution: explain the reason right in the form.
Metric: sign-up completion rate.
Add-on: a usability test to see whether the new explanation actually helped.
Now we have a clear connection between:
Research → Hypothesis → Design → Experiment → Metric → Learning
And most importantly: even when the experiment doesn't deliver the expected result, we learn something.
UX and Growth don't have to agree on everything
Working together doesn't mean the two areas will always share the same opinion.
And that's healthy.
Growth may push for a solution because they believe it can improve a metric.
UX may question whether that solution creates a bad experience.
Product may bring a business constraint.
Engineering may point out a technical limitation.
The team's job isn't to figure out who's right.
It's to find the best possible decision considering users, business and technology.
That's exactly why collaboration across areas matters so much.
In the end, we're talking about the same product
UX wants people to be able to use the product.
Growth wants more people to find value in the product and the business to grow.
Product needs both.
A product can have great conversion and a bad experience.
It can also have an excellent experience and fail to grow.
The challenge is finding the balance.
To me, the future of Product Design increasingly depends on this ability to connect the dots:
behavior + experience + data + business + technology.
We don't have to choose between UX or Growth.
We need to understand how the two can work together to build better products.

data.lead: Because in the end, sustainable growth shouldn't happen in spite of the user experience.
data.line: It should happen because of it.
